newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Short Australian debt rallies after data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Short Australian debt rallies after data.

text.p: *Short Australian bond and bills rallied as hopes of a further cut in official interest rates gathered pace following today's data showing a weak retail trade sector.
*Local long bonds also add to early U.S.-led price rises.

Short Australian bonds and bill futures rallied as hopes of a further cut in official interest rates gathered pace following today's data showing a weak retail sector, and could even push the Reserve Bank to ease this week.

Both December and fourth quarter retail trade data came in much weaker than expected, showing respective falls of 1.0 and 1.3 percent and in trend terms now stands at its weakest level in the 35-year history of the series.
"There's no denying that they are very soft numbers. It will lead to a somewhat softer GDP result for December quarter 1996," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
However, Roberts suspected the RBA would not make any immediate change in policy as it would want to see a bit more data before making a decision in March.

The RBA board held its first board meeting of the year today, and prior to today's data release the mood was fairly mixed as to whether it would endorse a policy easing given its concerns of the trade union's "living wage" claim.
But on the strength of today's data, Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank, feels that an imminent easing is definitely back on the agenda.
"If they were still meeting at the Reserve Bank, the data is likely to push them towards a February easing rather than March," James said.

March three-year bond futures rallied to 93.61 by the end of the morning session, up seven basis points on the day, and after dipping to 93.49 in early trading, while March bills also reversed an initial soft trend.
Meanwhile, the long-end added to their initial U.S.-led price gains, taking the benchmark 10-year bond yield to its lowest level since mid-December at around 7.32 percent.
The local rally saw the yield spreads wipe out most of the initial widening against U.S. and Canadian debt, and extended an early tightening to New Zealand.
U.S. Treasuries had rallied in New York on growing confidence that this week's FOMC will leave rates unchanged.
